title: Test Your Understanding: Back-of-the-Envelope Math
description: QPS, storage, bandwidth, and when estimates change architecture — not just memorizing constants.

questions.question: Why do back-of-the-envelope estimates come before detailed architecture?

options.text: Interviewers require exact spreadsheet precision before any diagrams
Order-of-magnitude QPS, storage, and bandwidth eliminate wrong designs and reveal the real bottleneck
They are only needed for write-heavy systems

questions.explanation: Napkin math is not about false precision. It tells you whether you're read-heavy vs write-heavy, whether data fits one node, and whether bandwidth or QPS dominates — so you pick cache, sharding, or queues for the right reason.

questions.question: Using the napkin shortcut (~100K seconds per day), what is the average QPS for 200 million requests per day?
questions.explanation: QPS_avg ≈ daily requests / 100,000. 200M / 100K = 2,000 QPS average. Peak is typically 2–3× that if traffic is uneven.

questions.question: 50M DAU each generate 40 requests per day. What is the approximate average QPS?
questions.explanation: Daily requests = 50M × 40 = 2B. QPS_avg = 2B / 100K = 20,000. The DAU × actions-per-day formula feeds directly into the 100K shortcut.

questions.question: In the URL shortener worked example (100M DAU, 0.1 new URLs/DAU/day, 5 redirects/DAU/day), what is the approximate read:write QPS ratio?
questions.explanation: Writes: 10M/day → ~100 QPS avg. Reads: 500M/day → ~5,000 QPS avg. Ratio ≈ 50:1 (often rounded to 100:1 in conversation). That conclusion drives cache-first design, not write-path tuning.

questions.question: A URL shortener stores ~20 billion mappings at ~600 bytes each, with 3× replication and ~25% headroom. Roughly how much total storage do you need?
questions.explanation: Raw ≈ 20B × 600 B ≈ 12 TB. With 3× replication ≈ 36 TB; plus ~25% headroom lands near ~45 TB — too large for one disk, sharding by short code becomes necessary.

questions.question: A system has ~5,000 average read QPS and ~100 average write QPS. Which design lever matters most for the redirect path?

options.text: Partitioning the write path into dozens of microservices first
Aggressive caching of hot short codes so most reads avoid disk
CDN for all API responses regardless of payload size
Strong consistency on every read from the primary database

questions.explanation: A 50:1 (or higher) read:write ratio means the read path is the product. Cache-aside for hot keys cuts DB load dramatically; write QPS at ~100/sec is modest by comparison.

questions.question: Which is a common back-of-the-envelope mistake?

options.text: Rounding 86,400 seconds per day to ~100K for mental math
Stating assumptions about DAU and actions per user explicitly
Using average QPS as peak load without a 2–3× multiplier
Multiplying storage by a replication factor

questions.explanation: Traffic is bursty — evenings, launches, and events concentrate load. Sizing only on average QPS under-provisions peak. Replication and headroom are correct to include; rounding to 100K is a standard shortcut.

questions.question: One user-facing page load always equals one QPS at the backend — fan-out to internal services does not affect capacity planning.
questions.explanation: A single page may trigger many internal RPCs, DB queries, and cache lookups. User-facing QPS × fan-out = backend QPS. Ignoring fan-out is a classic way to under-size gateways and databases.
